Fixture Manufacturing asks 100.00 dollars, within four dollars of its 52-week high of 104.00 and up sharply from the 61.00 low. The price already pays for the growth continuing.

The case against paying it starts with what the record cannot show. Capital spending is a declared gap, so free cash flow cannot be checked; a business can grow revenue 12.5 percent (900000000 against 800000000 a year earlier) while burning its cash on the machines that made the growth. One quarter of improvement, plus management's own unaudited outlook of 950000000, is the entire growth record in evidence. Everything else is extrapolation.

At a market value of 5200000000, the reported quarter's net income of 120000000 annualizes to roughly a 9.2 percent earnings yield only if the quarter repeats four times; the record proves one quarter, not four. Against a 4.10 percent one-month rate, the cushion is real but rests on that repetition. If demand flattens, the price has 40 percent of air below it down to the year's low. The declared gaps - capital spending and short interest - both sit exactly where this argument needs light.
